(Chris via Sam Harris and Jocko: courage is doing it despite fear; patience and motivation work the same.) He only talked about fitness and gyms once people kept asking: evidence changes how the world treats you. [▶ 2:05:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M4PzOjM5BJQ&t=7501s)
- **The gym floor** · Arrived in California with nowhere to stay; his mentor stood on a chair and asked the gym who'd house him ($400/month room). Then he slept on Astroturf in his empty gym under a parking garage, cars banging overhead like gunshots, college kids partying on the roof, living on naps for six months, shooing away homeless people. "It's a 30-second soundbite in my story, but it was years." First 29 members joined out of pity; first month he made $4,975 against $4,972 rent, watched it go to zero and had to do it again. Going back to his father would have meant his father's authority over his whole life, which felt like death. [▶ 2:11:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M4PzOjM5BJQ&t=7860s)
- **"Must be easy" = victim mindset** · You want it, but instead of feeling inadequate you blame an outside circumstance and give away all your agency. "I'd rather have absolute power and nothing to show for it than everything and no power." [▶ 2:16:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M4PzOjM5BJQ&t=8166s)
- **Uncertainty makes it worth it** · If you knew you'd succeed, it wouldn't be worth doing (the gods envied mortals). Who you're becoming is what you're amounting to, every day. [▶ 2:17:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M4PzOjM5BJQ&t=8227s)
- **The work you didn't put in** · (Mark Manson via Chris) Stop complaining about results from work you didn't do. Munger's prescription for failure: be inconsistent; it's very hard for consistent people not to succeed. In his gyms: "Out of the 21 meals, how many did you eat exactly as planned?" "At least half." Gym Launch value: do the boring work, boring makes you rich. 20 minutes of meeting prep makes you look 50 IQ points smarter; for one of his three consulting days he prepared 7 pages of money-making changes and the client said no one had ever prepared that much. [▶ 2:19:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M4PzOjM5BJQ&t=8342s)
- **The $7 kitchen timer** · His biggest focus tool: set it for the estimated task time, stop it the moment he checks his phone or Slack. Time on task is far lower than people think; most things are easier than they seem; people just don't know how to try hard. Define what would make failure unreasonable, then do those actions. [▶ 2:23:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M4PzOjM5BJQ&t=8582s)
- **Starting is the perfect condition** · Don't spend time getting in the mood; start. Elaborate morning routines were mental masturbation. Stop halfway through a sentence so the open loop pulls you back (Zeigarnik effect, Chris). [▶ 2:25:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M4PzOjM5BJQ&t=8705s)
- **There are no shortcuts for you** · Riff on Goggins. His normal day is 6–7am to ~6pm, 10–12 focused hours, 6.5 days a week (Saturday afternoon off); "triple shifts" add 8pm–1am during big pushes. His refrains: "I will do what is required" and "But I'll know." He's never regretted working harder. [▶ 2:28:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M4PzOjM5BJQ&t=8880s)
- **String good days together** · His first boss: happiness is stringing as many good days in a row as you can. His birthday looks like his Tuesday. A good day = worked hard on something worth doing + worked out + time with people he likes. (Chris: "Crush a Tuesday", Ferriss.) Successful people and others mean different things by "work": one hears joy, the other pain. [▶ 2:31:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M4PzOjM5BJQ&t=9062s)
- **If they don't have what you want, don't listen** · A relative at the holiday table: "I'd never live your life, you're so unbalanced." His health, marriage and money weren't. His answer now: "Good, don't. It's not your life." A mentor's trick: when someone says you're terrible, say "You're right" and move on. [▶ 2:35:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M4PzOjM5BJQ&t=9306s)
- **Don't play a game you didn't agree to** · (Chris: improv's "don't punk the game"; George Mack: "What's the point of having f-you freedom if you never say f-you?") A sign to cut a friend: they only talk about your past. Don't trade your self-respect for someone else's; it's easy to lose theirs and hard to get yours back. [▶ 2:38:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M4PzOjM5BJQ&t=9500s)
- **Paranoid now, faithful later** · "The cynics get to be right, the optimists get to be rich" (Sam Parr via Chris). His: the winner's mindset holds extreme paranoia in the present and unshakeable faith in the future. Doubters are right more often but not more right. They play the local status game; you're playing a wider one, so their opinions are noise. Most people in your life won't even make your funeral; why weigh their opinions while you're alive? [▶ 2:44:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M4PzOjM5BJQ&t=9846s)
- **Learning = same condition, new behaviour** · Intelligence = rate of learning. Life shows a red card and slaps you; if you don't duck next time, you didn't learn. The unhad conversation or put-off decision is the red card. That's why he cuts relationships he'll eventually cut: start enjoying the benefits today. [▶ 2:49:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M4PzOjM5BJQ&t=10143s)
- **$100M Leads** · 6 hours a day for two years, 19 drafts, 106 hand-drawn images; he advertised the book with every method in the book. Principles outlast platforms because humans don't change. [▶ 2:51:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M4PzOjM5BJQ&t=10262s)

lessons.t: 2026 · Modern Wisdom · The Life You Get When You Raise Your Standards (3h15) · 52 ideas
lessons.md:
> Watch it: [Modern Wisdom · The Life You Get When You Raise Your Standards (3h15)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ). 52 ideas, paraphrased in my words; ▶ jumps to the minute.

- **Control freak** · "Control freak is what people with low standards call people with high standards." You're not a control freak, you want it right the first time. Don't expect mediocre people to support world-class goals. If you have enough will it gets done your way anyway; less painful to do it right first. Great things come from one person who wouldn't let the idea be shaken out of them. [▶ 0:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=0s)
- **100 golden BBs** · There are no silver bullets, only hundreds of golden BBs: tiny improvements in a thousand details that someone checking a box won't bother with. The best art is made for yourself; thousands of people like you will get it. [▶ 2:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=122s)
- **High standards are a gift** · (Chris) He used to feel ashamed of being picky (a missing hyphen on a million cans); not stopping is probably why he's succeeded. Alex: big projects need one vision, otherwise you get Frankenstein copy-paste. He rehearsed his launch talk 3× a day for 30 days (100 run-throughs: out loud recorded, watch and edit, repeat). The first 5 reps make you better; the next 95 make a masterpiece, and that's where everyone drops off. [▶ 4:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=240s)
- **Regression to the mean kills your edge** · Others pull high-standard people back toward comfortable. Companies decay when founders leave: 100 BBs → 99 → 98, and three years later the magic's gone. The founder/host is the hub who sees everything. [▶ 7:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=424s)
- **Real perfectionists finish** · Most self-labelled perfectionists are procrastinating. Real ones itch until it's done and work every hour on it; if you can't say how your thing is getting better, you're not a perfectionist, you're ignorant. Pick your battles: no compromise on the highest-contribution items, volume on low-leverage stuff (shorts, tweets). [▶ 9:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=544s)
- **The pottery class** · Graded on one perfect pot vs graded on quantity: the quantity class made better pots. Volume negates luck. One "perfect" first podcast has no data behind it; 1,000 podcasts give you the perspective to judge. [▶ 12:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=724s)
- **Getting older without getting better** · = relearning the same lesson. Learning = same condition, new behaviour. To founders: hands up if you work all hours… keep them up if your revenue's been flat 6+ months. Same hands: you're doing the wrong stuff. Exposure isn't learning; recall and application are. [▶ 14:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=843s)
- **One book, then do it all** · After ~10 self-help books he still lived in the same Baltimore condo with the same job; he committed not to read another book until he'd done everything in the current one, which is when he quit. He reads little non-fiction because one chapter can take two weeks to implement. Win or learn: knowing that ≠ knowing how (100 books on sales vanish on your first cold call). [▶ 18:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=1085s)
- **Copycats know the what, not the why** · A photocopier isn't an artist. Fear the day nobody copies you. Gym Launch ran an R&D department testing a "play" every 14 days ($50–100k each; ~70% lost to control) and shared the failures with licensees. Copiers are 3–6 months late and can't adapt when conditions change; you win in the weeds. [▶ 22:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=1322s)
- **Exceptional means different** · You can't fit in and be exceptional; both hurt (internal conflict vs external). "When friends say you've changed, they don't know how to say you've grown." Old people are happier because they don't have time for drama; start being that way now. He was more miserable pleasing everyone than he is with everyone unhappy with him; he speaks to no one from his pre-quitting life. [▶ 27:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=1620s)
- **Think for yourself, then check your maths** · By the time there's consensus it's mispriced. The value you'd compute alone in a room, believed over everyone else's, after double-checking. "Yes, you're all wrong" needs evidence behind it. [▶ 32:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=1927s)
- **100 days of rejection** · (Chris) Ask for a free coffee etc.; at day 100 you're still alive. Sales and club promo teach that rejection doesn't kill you. [▶ 40:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=2407s)
- **Known ≠ respected** · Don't sacrifice your values for views ("dance monkey dance"); make it for you and the 10 people who care and the hits follow. More creators fade from becoming cringe than irrelevant (Chris). There's no return policy on integrity. The only forever-not-cringe thing is authenticity; forever-cringe is pandering, especially for personal gain. Authenticity = alignment of what you think, say and do; fix bad thoughts rather than faking. [▶ 42:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=2527s)
- **What would you do if you weren't afraid?** · His life goal is to be fearless. Content rule: "one of one" (only things only we can make: "I doubled this company's sales with these four things", never a Coca-Cola breakdown), which became "one of zero" (things we didn't know we could do yet). He's never regretted failures, only things he didn't try. [▶ 51:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=3061s)
- **Play it out two steps** · Quitting was his hardest decision; his fallback was "at worst I'll have a great story for business school". Worst case: a friend's floor, then Uber (~$70–80k) and stripping (~$150–200k). Leila: "Fear is a mile wide and an inch deep." [▶ 53:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=3185s)
- **"But I'll know" vs "what will they think?"** · Excellence is making "but I'll know" more important than everyone else's opinion: breaking what everyone else calls beautiful to make it how you want. People who settle while knowing better end up hating themselves; they lock the door on the better man clearing his throat next door. [▶ 58:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=3483s)
- **Leverage vs violence** · There's a time for leverage and a time for violence (brute force). Optimal = most bang for buck; maximising = most bucks. Seasons of no: say no to almost everything for an extended period. "Unbalanced" is meant as an insult but it's true, and that's the point: balance never gives outsized returns. (Chris: a man called Leila a "skinny b—"; she took it as a compliment.) For their first three years married he told Leila the business came before the marriage; later they flipped it. [▶ 59:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=3580s)
- **Choose in advance what you'll suck at** · (Burkeman via Chris) With "the curse of competence", options are limited by what you choose, not what you can do. Gains are multiplicative, not additive: periodise. "Now isn't forever." [▶ 1:04:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=3846s)
- **Which problems would we prefer?** · For big decisions they list the problems each path brings (bad reviews, a favourite customer telling them off) and pick the problems they're better equipped for. Regret comes from imagining the unchosen path with only its upside (Midnight Library). Remembering the downsides you avoided minimises post-decision regret. [▶ 1:06:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=3961s)
- **Optimisation becomes superstition** · He's a maximiser, not an optimiser: if n gives x, can we do 1,000n? He loves competing with people who "need" 8 hours, a morning routine, supplements, coffee: fragile and easy to break. North star: a laptop, internet and a folding chair. A sleep ring made him chase sleep PRs and sleep worse. Two years of gym turnarounds on gas-station food was for then, not forever. "List everything you won't give up for your dream; that's what the person who beats you will give up." [▶ 1:09:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=4145s)
- **Find someone who gets your peculiarities** · Being yourself means many people find you weird and there's no second date, which is fine. On their first date (frozen yoghurt) he broke down how the shop made money and Leila joined in: "Wait, you see this too?" The alternative is someone falling for a role you must perform forever. Robert Glover via Chris: an attractive man is comfortable in his own skin, knows where he's going and has fun getting there; even one of the three works. [▶ 1:13:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=4385s)
- **Everyone dies anyway** · "Murder only changes when, not whether": no need for vendettas. Insults that hurt are the ones you believe. [▶ 1:18:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=4681s)
- **Agree and one-up** · The stoic response to hate: agree and one-up ("if you knew half of it you'd think worse"). Agreement extinguishes conflict, like a slot machine paying nothing. If an insult stings, there's some truth; agree. Life goal: die with no secrets, so everyone's in one room and people like or hate the real him. [▶ 1:21:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=4866s)
- **False accusations: be louder with the truth** · (Chris via Rob Henderson: reputational damage is real even when false.) Alex: if it's true, agree and one-up; if false but damaging, don't address the person, be ten times louder with the truth through your actions (his college reputation). Portnoy came out swinging because he hadn't done it. [▶ 1:26:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=5164s)
- **You can only be cancelled if you agree** · Unless every channel removes you, you choose to be cancelled by stopping. Chris disagrees ("cancellation makes you bigger" is cope; deplatforming works). Everyone only remembers your last four streams (Destiny). [▶ 1:31:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=5467s)
- **Only one person in the angry boat** · At 18, at a fur-coat dealer, an angry customer came in; the owner got angrier than her on her behalf ("who sold you this? they'll never eat again") and she calmed right down. When everyone's angry at you, roast yourself harder than they can. [▶ 1:36:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=5765s)
- **Maybe you're just sensitive** · "You can't wish for a strong character and an easy life; each is the price of the other." Ten-years-ago problems look tiny now; ten years from now, today's will too. His first lawsuit felt huge; Tesla always has hundreds. Problems are evidence you're on the chosen path. (Chris: his old journal entry panicking about an MC leaving.) [▶ 1:38:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=5910s)
- **Push or pivot** · Invest vs consume is a continuum to manage, not a problem to solve. His rule: don't quit unless new information shows an original assumption was wrong. Everything except stopping is a pivot. Decide leading indicators up front (e.g. content: business topics nobody else covers will slowly find an audience) so you can keep pushing before the outcome. [▶ 1:43:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=6184s)
- **Work without seeing results** · The world belongs to those who can keep working without seeing results. Extend the time horizon on things most people can't weather. Elite lifters are the ones who come in every day without getting bored (Clear via Chris); Fraser isn't fired up for Zone 2, he just does it. "Do the boring work; boring makes you rich": follow up with every lead. Most successful people's Rocky cut-scene lasts 5–10 years. [▶ 1:47:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=6423s)
- **Hard = no one else will do it** · Train how you respond to hard: from "warning sign" to "selection effect". Flip "poor me" to "poor everyone else who has to try". [▶ 1:50:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=6630s)
- **Be the single clap** · People only root for those who don't need it. For a long time it's a slow clap from one person: you. If everyone's cheering, you're like everyone else. [▶ 1:52:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=6750s)
- **It won't get harder than the start** · (Chris) 85% of his listeners found him in 2023, after 600 episodes; one December beat the first 3.5 years. Protect your passion, because the rewards per unit of effort are highest later. Alex: the beginning is you with a stick against a bear; later dragons are bigger but you have allies, money and leverage. No one can work out or learn for you. Slumdog Millionaire / Jobs' calligraphy: skills from the trenches become arrows in the quiver. [▶ 1:54:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=6847s)
- **Experts have more ways to win** · (Dr Kashy) Experts get many fast feedback loops before the final outcome. Early on, make who you're becoming the asset: each long day makes you the person who can work 5 years without reward. Future-cast the story you'll tell; he screenshotted his empty bank account: "this won't happen again". [▶ 1:59:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=7144s)
- **Most epic story razor** · Rogan's "be the hero of your movie". Alex told a portfolio founder: to predict me, ask what would make the most epic story (sell Gym Launch, marry Leila, live at the gym, a media company that gives everything away, a billionaire who documented the whole way). Videos with 5 views are breadcrumbs for later. Until you win, effort goes unnoticed; get used to it. [▶ 2:04:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=7442s)
- **Messenger and message are linked** · (Chris: same line went viral 6 years later.) A self-deprecating joke from the class clown lands; from the straight-A athlete it doesn't. [▶ 2:07:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=7626s)
- **Authority is lazy consumption** · A teacher giving Buffett's advice is ignored because he didn't build Berkshire; people use authority so they don't have to process the idea. To get there, disagree with people for a long time until you're proven right. (Sutherland via Chris: nobody gets fired for hiring KPMG.) The line between charlatan and visionary is often just the outcome (Fyre Festival). [▶ 2:09:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=7741s)
- **Too good to fail** · Sales because you sucked at marketing, marketing because you sucked at product. If you open a sandwich shop, make the sandwich so good the rest doesn't matter. Find the one big domino that makes everything else irrelevant. [▶ 2:14:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=8042s)
- **You don't find passion, you create it** · Start by doing something you suck at → get good → like it → people ask how you found your passion. When he started the gym, his "passion" became work. Set the expectation that everything sucks, then become the person who does it anyway. (Chris: turning pro at what you love = pickleball when you're hungover, cold, tired; is that a price you'll pay?) [▶ 2:16:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=8164s)
- **Model the climb, not the summit** · His current day (6h writing, 2h calls, his custom gym, dinner with Leila, read in a recliner) is what he does now, not how he got here: "I did a ton of stuff I hate for a long time with nobody rooting for me." Ask successful people what they did at your stage. [▶ 2:20:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=8403s)
- **Ruthless dollars per hour** · After his first $500 sale in 30 minutes he decided anything worth less than ~$250/30min he'd hand off: no more cooking, groceries or cleaning. Before opening gyms 7–10 he filmed a video saying he'd give up football and Netflix, all he had left after evenings and Sundays. Write the list of what you'll sacrifice, not a to-do list. Seinfeld: two hours daily where he's not allowed to do anything else. The ultimate productivity hack is "no". [▶ 2:23:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=8587s)
- **If miserable either way, be miserable building something** · Circumstance doesn't set wellbeing (monks). Victor Hugo had his servant lock him in a cold room until he slid 6 pages under the door (Chris; apps like Opal). [▶ 2:26:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=8790s)
- **Goal: do epic stuff, not be happy** · His goal is to be useful and do epic things; what he sacrificed longest pays the biggest memory dividends. Obsessing over happiness made him depressed; he said "forget happiness, I'll just do stuff" and a few days later noticed he wasn't miserable. Wanting to be happier creates the gap that makes you unhappy. (Chris: Kahneman over Gilbert — a good life is one you're glad you lived. Peterson: "take more of what poisons you until it becomes a tonic.") [▶ 2:28:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=8910s)
- **If you don't have it, you're not worthy yet** · Better to know you're bad for a season than pretend you're good for a lifetime. You're not making the money you want because you're not as good as you think. Imposter syndrome = you're a student pretending to be a teacher. "You are worthy" affirmations: the test is whether you have it. Give yourself permission to suck, be unhappy, lose friends, be an exception so you can become exceptional. [▶ 2:36:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=9361s)
- **State the facts and tell the truth** · The best marketing is truth; if your truth isn't compelling, don't lie, change the world so the facts become compelling. The 18-year-old "motivational speaker" should list what a speaker would need to have done, and do it. You feel like an impostor because you know. A big new bet stated honestly ("I could be wrong") isn't impostorhood. [▶ 2:39:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=9545s)
- **Mood without reasons** · If you can be in a bad mood for no reason, you can be in a good one for no reason. If it won't change your life, it shouldn't change your mood. If the cost is peace of mind, don't buy it. [▶ 2:43:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=9780s)
- **Cynicism is short-term rightness** · At Acquisition.com they check their "no bias": saying no is always right short-term and wrong in the one way that matters. Your family is right about every girl until your wife. They measure in days, you measure in decades. His first nine businesses failed. (Chris: the cynical genius illusion.) Trevor (his editor): "99% right, 100% wrong." [▶ 2:44:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=9870s)
- **Peace of mind = values check** · A VC posted a clip attacking him; Alex DM'd and dismantled it; the VC admitted he'd done it to go viral, which disgusts Alex. Chris walked back 30 yards to bin a wrapper: "you'd know." [▶ 2:51:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=10264s)
- **Tell the truth socially** · Challenge: decline invites with "I don't want to" instead of a fake excuse. "Would you prefer I lied to you?" Cut niceties so your words carry weight (team knows a compliment is real). When someone says "make sense?" and it doesn't, say no; looking stupid for a moment beats being stupid for life. [▶ 2:56:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=10560s)
- **Not knowing is growth** · If you knew what you were doing, it wouldn't be growth. He's strongly against reflexive mental-health medication and "something's wrong with you" labels (his view, stated as an extreme stance; not medical advice). Deal with the thing you're worried about. You can't want growth and certainty, strong character and an easy life. [▶ 2:59:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=10770s)
- **Your evidence is your message** · 900-follower accounts teaching growth: your evidence disproves your words before you speak. A fitness coach who isn't in shape: get shredded, the one big domino. [▶ 3:07:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=11227s)
- **Trauma, defined** · A punishing event that permanently changes behaviour; it's accelerated learning. To change behaviour back, create new conditions that reinforce the new behaviour. 100 calls > "putting out a frequency". [▶ 3:09:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=11370s)
- **Skool bet** · His biggest investment ever: co-owner of Skool, because education is broken and communities are hard to automate. [▶ 3:12:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gk8EGWoGnEQ&t=11550s)

lessons.t: 2026 · Modern Wisdom · Success Is Just a Side Effect of Following These Principles (1h45, 2023) · 27 ideas
lessons.md:
> Watch it: [Modern Wisdom · Success Is Just a Side Effect of Following These Principles (1h45, 2023)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8). 27 ideas, paraphrased in my words; ▶ jumps to the minute.

- **Nothing going for you = nothing to lose** · Every position has advantages: small players are nimble and personal. If you have nothing, you can take many risks fast and end up where you are: zero. Lower downside should lower your action threshold. (Jack Butcher via Chris: get rich taking big risks with small money, stay rich taking small risks with big money.) [▶ 1:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=64s)
- **Name the one voice** · What people fear losing is imaginary: what others will think. Six questions deep it's usually one person ("Uncle Harry"): "Will Uncle Harry's opinion be why you live below your potential forever?" Shame only lives in the shadows; drag it into the light (your mom's comment at Thanksgiving vs 60 years of resentment). [▶ 3:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=183s)
- **Nobody sees you fail early** · (Chris) A flopped club night is seen by 150 people. Alex: treat early content as practice, preseason. Track lots of stats: the more ways you track, the more ways you win. Treat impressions as a room: 100 people would be a great room; 13 views is a small room. Watch relative growth (10→15 followers = +50%) and project it forward. [▶ 6:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=364s)
- **More skills = more ways to reward yourself** · (Dr Kashy) Successful people don't have more willpower; they find more ways to reward themselves. Travis Mash logs every lift at every weight and rep so lifters PR every session. [▶ 11:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=667s)
- **Change your environment** · Easiest fix when life sucks; even two miles down the road or moving out of your mom's basement counts. Vietnam heroin: users who came home relapsed far less than typical addicts, because the cues were gone. Clinic → same environment → same behaviour. Chris uses different spots for different tasks (emails on a desk bike = 3h Zone 2 a week). To start a habit, remove its punishment and add cues: a no-touch sunscreen dispenser at each of his three "watering holes". [▶ 13:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=785s)
- **Distractions come dressed as easy opportunities** · Businesses die of indigestion, not starvation. Entrepreneurs learn the wrong lesson ("changing direction works") from early pivots. The woman in the red dress gets hotter as you grow. When he met Leila he had nine spinning plates (chiro agency, dental agency, five gyms, Gym Launch turnarounds), all break-even, him as CEO of all. The most successful say no to almost everything (Buffett). [▶ 19:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=1145s)
- **Obvious thing, extraordinary time** · "Success = doing the obvious thing for an extraordinary period of time without convincing yourself you're smarter than you are": thinking you're smart makes you take on more. (Chris: "You can't overestimate the unimportance of practically everything"; Essentialism.) Specialise in projects, generalise in skills as you grow. [▶ 22:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=1350s)
- **Conquer tiny impulses** · The first step to a massive dream is conquering tiny impulses. No successes yet? You got dressed, you sat at the computer: smaller evidence still counts; stack it. (Chris: "imposter adaptation" — if you keep disproving the imposter voice and it persists, it's a habit, not your ability; competence without confidence vs confidence without competence.) [▶ 26:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=1560s)
- **Compare risks, don't try to eliminate them** · Good opportunities only look like opportunities in hindsight; today they look like risk. There's always a reason to say no; even Treasuries carry risk. Use risk-adjusted return. His order for picking opportunities: (1) highest likelihood with no new skills and no new effort, (2) more effort but no new skills, (3) only then learn a new skill, choosing the highest-leverage one. Learn decision-making from investors: they have a scoreboard. [▶ 30:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=1807s)
- **"This is what hard feels like"** · As fraternity president, every pledge class revolted on day 10–14. He asked: who wanted this? Who thought it'd be easy? Who thought hard? "Guys, this is what hard feels like." Expectations reset, and permission to feel bad made them stop feeling bad. "This is where most people stop, and why they don't win." (Chris: Cam Hanes carries a rock marked "poser" up a hill unfilmed; 90% of podcasts die before episode 3, 90% of the rest before 20; 21 episodes puts you in the top percentile.) [▶ 34:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=2040s)
- **Burnout vs emotional burnout** · Real burnout = output per unit of time dropping (measurable; he slumps 6–7 hours into recording). What most call burnout is a comment that stung: drag it into the light; is this comment bigger than my future? Ask "what if they're right?" (Byron Katie via Chris: "is it true?") Tom Bilyeu has big ears: true; still makes content. "I don't need to deserve success to get it." [▶ 42:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=2522s)
- **The bar is low** · Goggins/Dana White via Chris: people are weak, so a weekend savage runs them over. Use that as market information. [▶ 47:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=2827s)
- **Poverty's first lesson: "my fault"** · At 19 he realised blaming his parents gave people he hated power over his success. If you suffered real inequality or abuse you'd be justified in not achieving, but you can be the local proof that someone had it worse and did better. Power follows the blame finger. Not your fault? Doesn't matter: put the prosthetic on and run. [▶ 48:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=2910s)
- **From aphorism to action** · Two things: know the input→output equation down to the first concrete action (make the call, post the piece, run the ad, put the shoes on); then know what your fuel will be. [▶ 51:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=3065s)
- **Use what you have: pain as fuel** · He watched TED talks and read a self-help book a night with zero change (mental masturbation). One book said there are "entrepreneurs and wantrepreneurs"; it stung because it was true. Most people lack passion but have pain, anger or shame: use that first. His fuel was hatred of his current existence and of living his dad's dream: "Sometimes your parents' dreams have to die for yours to live." [▶ 53:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=3187s)
- **Negative visualisation** · Pain moves people more than pleasure. Instead of positive visualisation he future-casts: if I keep doing this for 10 more years, what does my life look like? That magnifies current pain until it crosses the action threshold. [▶ 56:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=3362s)
- **His dad's apology** · Taking home ~$1.5M/month at 27, his dad called: "I'm sorry, for everything." Alex felt nothing and said "I won't thank you on stage because you didn't believe in me"; dad replied "We'll see how long it lasts." Realisation: he'd been winning his dad's game (money = worth), so he had to define his own game and rules. [▶ 59:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=3543s)
- **Infinite games** · (Sinek) Applying finite rules to infinite games fails (Vietnam). Fitness, marriage, business and success are infinite: the point of the game is to keep playing. His version of winning: define a perfect day and live as many in a row as possible. [▶ 1:03:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=3782s)
- **Champions are broken** · Three common traits of the hyper-successful: superiority complex, crippling insecurity, impulse control (big cheese, big tiger, stay on the path). Dr Kashy: champions don't have something extra, they lack an off button. So ask: what problem are you solving? Contentment doesn't need all that; richest-man-in-the-world does. [▶ 1:06:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=3964s)
- **It's play for him** · Criticised for no hobbies: "I don't want any." Everything he does is the game (podcast, books, drawings, deals). Chris: Steffi Graf tested 10/10 on both skill and desire to train; what looks like work to you may be play to someone else. "The person who loves walking walks further than the person who loves the destination." He's averse to punishment and just stacks rewarding activities. [▶ 1:10:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=4230s)
- **Directionally correct beats absolutely correct** · You can't find "your thing" without perspective; try many things fast. Most people have more cat than cheese: run away from the cat and you'll probably get closer to cheese. He picked between frozen yogurt, test prep and a gym; moved to the furthest place from Baltimore; avoided what he hated (meetings, meaningless grunt work). (Chris: the reverse role model; Munger: avoid being stupid.) [▶ 1:17:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=4625s)
- **Never underestimate your opponent** · "You gain nothing from underestimating your opponent" (from a portfolio CEO's "we're way better than them"). Only hubris topples the one at the top. 20 minutes of prep makes you look much smarter; not preparing only buys looking naturally gifted. Assume you're always the underdog: only the paranoid survive. [▶ 1:22:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=4923s)
- **Copycats need you** · Beat copiers by getting bigger, not by fighting. They can at best be the second-best Alex. Original content comes from documenting your real life (his tweets come from real meetings). [▶ 1:25:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=5103s)
- **Egos keep more people poor** · There are far more rich anonymous people than Lambo-flaunters; ~98% of online business gurus sell platform-building. Real operators are humble because they've repeatedly felt inadequate at new levels. Keep an ego only by staying a big fish in a small pond: face harder bosses. He compares himself daily to Buffett's net worth by age. You can't admit your deficits and claim greatness at once. [▶ 1:27:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=5250s)
- **Fewer people at the top** · Less square footage at the top of the mountain, but those people have more context; most people only have 2–3 good relationships anyway. While climbing you keep changing strata, so friendships are more transient; only a problem if you hate it. [▶ 1:33:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=5585s)
- **AI and social** · Predicted (2023): AI content everywhere, verification will come to mean "real human". (Chris: algorithms programme users; audience capture.) [▶ 1:37:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=5826s)
- **$100M Leads stats** · ~3,500 combined hours with his editor over two years; first 4–6 hours of every day. [▶ 1:44:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JuNOFW-oVn8&t=6240s)

lessons.t: 2026 · Diary of a CEO (Steven Bartlett) · Stop Chasing AI, Build This Instead (2h20, 2026) · 40 ideas
lessons.md:
> Watch it: [Diary of a CEO (Steven Bartlett) · Stop Chasing AI, Build This Instead (2h20, 2026)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c). 40 ideas, paraphrased in my words; ▶ jumps to the minute.

- **Emotional discomfort isn't a reason to change course** · After a ~$106M launch his mother saw it, then died four weeks later; his tweets in that period were notes to himself ("I just have to keep fighting"). People judge love by how much you choose to suffer; the person you lost probably doesn't want that. In business and life: "My emotional discomfort is not an adequate reason to change what I'm doing." [▶ 0:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=0s)
- **14 years compressed** · 1) Decide whether you care more about your future than what others think of it: someone's version of you has to die. 2) The fastest way to $10M isn't the fastest way to $100M; focus and patience are the two enduring advantages because they're so anti-human. [▶ 1:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=60s)
- **AI in the wrong places** · Ask the AI-maxers: are you making more money? A business paid 11 VAs ~$11k/month, then spent $350k (3+ years of their cost) building AI to replace them, though it wasn't the constraint; they needed customers. Don't start or advertise as an "AI business"; use AI in your business and sell the outcome. Many customers fear AI. [▶ 3:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=186s)
- **Value left when intelligence is cheap** · Someone has to own the decision and the risk (AI pays no taxes, owns no LLC). Humans want stakes: a fake $5M MrBeast prize means nothing; chess is more popular than ever despite engines; nobody watches F1 without Hamilton in the car. [▶ 5:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=307s)
- **Don't outsource thinking** · Ask Claude, ChatGPT and others the same decision and they're all over the place; you can get AI to agree to anything. Delegate your hardest thinking and you get dumber fast: "this brain is the best asset I've got, so I keep it sharp." [▶ 7:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=427s)
- **Build for 50 years** · The blocks exercise: build the tallest tower in 30 seconds vs 5 minutes vs 5 years with unlimited blocks, and the foundation changes completely. Since deciding Acquisition.com is "forever", he makes different decisions and obsesses over "the factory" (Elon: the prototype is easy, the factory is 50× harder; Tesla built its own batteries and chargers; Bezos made logistics Amazon's moat). Founders who rush for an exit build unstable towers, skyrocket, plateau, then must step back to rebuild the foundation. "I have no announcement this month because I'm doing boring things like hiring." [▶ 8:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=520s)
- **Stay longer in product-market fit** · The $1M founder who can't reach $10M usually churns everyone: Company B sells 100, 200, 300 a year and loses them all ($3M, needs 600 new next year); Company A sells 100 a year and keeps them ($3M with 300 customers). Invest in A every time; acquisition cost compounds against B. Great marketing and sales can be dangerous: they hide a hole in the back of the bus until sales stop and it craters. [▶ 14:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=845s)
- **"I've run out of time"** · First question: what's your margin? Thin margin is the root cause: the offer is mispriced (too much for too little) or there's no sales motion that shows the value. Founders "sell out of their own wallet": what's easy for you isn't easy for them. 70% margin? Hire help. [▶ 17:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=1026s)
- **No unicorns** · "No one can do it like me" is ego; the business's job is to serve customers, not your need to be needed. Teach the job as if you were going back in time: a tenth of the time it took you. Stop looking for a unicorn; get a rhino (horn), a horse and fireflies (sparkle): find in three people what you can't find in one. His hiring mistake: bar not high enough. In every department the highest person should hold the highest standard; if someone's standard beats yours, they should run it. [▶ 19:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=1170s)
- **"What have you done so far?"** · When people pitch ideas, his reply: "What have you done so far?" Usually nothing. Starting a business is four steps: LLC, bank account, a way to take money, ask a stranger if you can do something for them for money. That changes your identity from wantrepreneur to entrepreneur, like a first purchase does for a customer. [▶ 23:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=1385s)
- **Advice to younger self** · Ideally his future self would say nothing because it worked. Otherwise: everything early is fear, which is justified; the only way to know is to start. The fog clears a couple of steps ahead; only take the steps you can see. You must embrace cringe. Staying put is the one path with a 100% chance of not getting what you want. Fear and confusion only exist in the vague: what does failure actually mean? 100 noes, change the offer, 100 more. Worst case: a friend's couch, move home to extend the runway. He split a bedroom for $400 with a mattress on the floor; people are handcuffed to their lifestyle. [▶ 25:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=1530s)
- **More doors, not fewer** · (Bartlett) Success multiplies doors and uncertainty. Alex: it's never easier to know what to do than at the start; the problem is whose voice you're obeying. He nearly didn't sell Gym Launch for $46M because one acquaintance might not think it was "legit". [▶ 30:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=1830s)
- **The six-month leap** · He nearly went to Booth for an MBA: ~$240k opportunity cost vs "can I get to $10k/month in two years?" He couldn't answer "how will an MBA help your long-term goals?" in three days. A book every two days, no change; nightly 2–3h calls with a friend about businesses, pacing a hole in his IKEA rug. His dad kept talking him down ("you're following the plan"), so he drove halfway across the country before calling. His dad's story: fled the Iranian revolution, failed med school twice in French, ran X-ray slides for two years, built his own surgery centre to spec from Home Depot, then went through an ugly divorce. Dad's view now: "a year or two is nothing; you won't even remember it." Alex was terrified of winning the lottery because he couldn't prove he could do it himself; he self-funded. [▶ 33:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=2010s)
- **Is entrepreneurship for you?** · Be specific about the goal and what it changes in your daily life. "Freedom" is often options-maxing, but the best parts of life come after you walk through one door and leave the others: commitment. People get stuck at crossroads; unmade decisions last forever while feedback loops move you. You change when staying the same hurts more than changing (Robbins). [▶ 40:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=2400s)
- **Hard ≠ valuable** · A hard problem isn't necessarily a valuable one (a hard marathon pays nothing). To be a millionaire you don't need a hard problem: just serve a badly-served market slightly better (a pool cleaner who shows up on time and knocks on doors). [▶ 46:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=2790s)
- **Reality is the moat** · With AI slop flooding content, the moat is reality: brand, reputation and track record that only exist in real life. Musk, Bezos, Buffett are the biggest business influencers because they own the businesses; a teacher quoting Buffett word for word won't get the views. His change: only do things only he can do (hundreds of $1M+ owners flying in monthly for live advice; real stakes). Entertainment is consumed, education changes behaviour; the higher the risk of acting on advice (beauty < personal finance < business), the more people demand credibility. (Bartlett: hard and scarce.) [▶ 47:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=2870s)
- **Avoid commoditised tips without proof** · The big "why should I listen to you?" Authority lowers the effort of consuming information. Starting out? Document proof of effort (MrBeast counting to a huge number): film your whole sales day, clip the best moment of 22 calls. [▶ 54:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=3240s)
- **Value equation applied** · Dream outcome × perceived likelihood ÷ (time delay × effort & sacrifice). Effort = what you must start doing; sacrifice = the good things you must stop. A $19 PDF vs a $3k trainer: likelihood is the difference. Most slept-on lever: time; do what everyone else does in half the time and someone will pay a premium. Bezos: bet on what won't change (lower prices, more selection, faster delivery). People discount distant guaranteed outcomes to zero (index funds vs today's latte). [▶ 56:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=3364s)
- **Unwitnessable lessons** · Consistency (an employee who'd watched his content for years only got it seeing him at the office at 6am every day), focus ("people only see the choices you made, not the options you had", Sharran) and patience (nobody watches the middle of a marathon). Steve Wynn: the best thing for a casino is a first-time big win; he hopes beginners get one big reward for delayed gratification early. Bartlett: 1,000 Instagram posts → 1,000 followers, then +300k in three posts; slow then fast. More mistakes come from abandoning the right path than picking the wrong one. [▶ 1:01:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=3660s)
- **Push vs pivot** · Pivot only if a fundamental assumption has been proven untrue by your activities; otherwise push. Bartlett's test: am I giving even a tiny group scarce value? (his friend asking "when's the next episode?") [▶ 1:04:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=3880s)
- **Unscalable first, priced high** · "That's not scalable." "You're broke; you can just make money." Your future self will have skills to scale it. Start with the most absurdly valuable thing: add one or two zeros to your price and list what you'd need to do to be worth it (go to their house, grocery shop, drive them to the gym; you only need five clients at $100k). Benefits: better customers, learning from people richer than you (like caddies), real data nobody else has, and a high anchor ("for those who can't afford my private clients…"), the Tesla Roadster → Model S path. You're trying to solve tomorrow's problems with today's resources; future you will have more. "As long as you don't quit, take feedback and improve over a long enough horizon, you win." Quit the doggy-skateboard, not business: local vs global failure. [▶ 1:06:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=3990s)
- **Behaviourism for self-awareness** · If what you want isn't happening, your model of the world is wrong. Grandpa won't take his pill: don't say "you can't make a horse drink"; crush it into cold lemonade with salty peanuts and his favourite backgammon game. Arrange conditions; don't persuade. [▶ 1:13:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=4384s)
- **300 flyers vs 150,000** · A mentor with 22 locations asked his test size: Alex put out 300 flyers; the mentor tests 5,000 per batch, then 3,000 a day (~150k a month). People 100 steps ahead often do 100× the volume. The pain of inefficiency is what pushes you to systematise, and that scarce, unglamorous work becomes your edge. [▶ 1:15:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=4530s)
- **Incentives explain everything** · Ask why they aren't: what incentives are they deciding within? Copy structure: do the thing → more good, less bad; don't → less good, more bad; ping-pong between them. Telling staff "adopt AI" fails if their incentives reward the old job (Innovator's Dilemma). Gary Halbert: don't create demand, channel it. [▶ 1:17:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=4650s)
- **Who do you serve?** · At first take anyone with a pulse and a card. Between $1M and $3M decide which customers are easiest and pay most ("we help doctors get patients using podcasts"): one thing for many, cut once sell twice. [▶ 1:21:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=4890s)
- **Where the opportunities are** · Old-school Meta ad agencies are saturated; newer plays: Reddit reputation management, clipping agencies, AI automation for small businesses. Bet on what won't change: looking good and young (longevity, med spa, peptides), wealth advisers, insurance, and "uncool" businesses nobody wants to mention at parties (waste, elder care). A $20M restaurant owner could make $200M with the same skills in a better vehicle. Wealth is concentrated: bottom 50% hold ~2% of US wealth, top 1% ~31%; beginners sell to people with no money and conclude nobody has money. [▶ 1:23:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=5010s)
- **Price tracks how good you are** · In services, price correlates almost 1:1 with how advanced the business is: deliver more value than you charge → demand exceeds supply → raise price → repeat. A $2k/month social agency can't even handle him; his minimum vendor is ~$15k/month. Higher prices: better customers, better margins, less headache, signals skill. Van Westendorp pricing (too expensive / too cheap / expensive-but-buy / bargain), now runnable with AI in minutes; slice by customer type (sometimes two humps). [▶ 1:28:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=5310s)
- **Every problem is a marketing problem** · ~70% of $1–50M businesses he sees are demand-constrained, ~30% supply-constrained. The supply side mirrors the customer funnel: application generation → nurture → interview (the sale) → onboarding → retention → ascension. Look at your job posts and outreach copy and you'll be horrified. Every Acquisition.com applicant watches a 13-minute VSL about the company; use interview scripts and role-play like sales; 30/60/90 onboarding; career paths. Ask your best people (and customers): "What would it take for you to stay forever?" [▶ 1:33:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=5580s)
- **Price the referral by its value** · A ~$10M brokerage paid $500 for agent referrals; a mentor asked what a productive agent makes in gross profit ($250k/yr) and suggested $25k per referral. The company went from $10M to $400M. Headhunters for exceptional talent are always a deal. [▶ 1:37:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=5825s)
- **People are the best and worst decisions** · What changed most: much higher talent standards and less tolerance for keeping mediocre people. A $100B-company founder: at 20 hiring mattered, at 30 it was important, at 40 it's the single most important thing. Marrying Leila: "probably the single best financial decision I ever made"; she believed in him more than he did ("good thing you're the best at it"). He still has doubts; the pressure feels the same at every level, only the resources grow: early on it's a bear barehanded, later a dragon with an army. Leila bet on the jockey when he was a 26-year-old gym owner. [▶ 1:38:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=5920s)
- **Apathy, not anxiety** · His struggle is apathy ("we have enough money, why bother?"); at some point last year he felt it was enough, like stopping at ~250 lb lean. Leila's dream was to build a place people love to work; she's the pure operator, the reason talent stays, and carried him through motivation troughs. [▶ 1:42:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=6160s)
- **Partner unsupportive?** · Figure out what you want; there are trades. He speaks from maximising business outcomes, which differs from maximising wellbeing. Arthur Brooks: a Ferrari to a 3-star Michelin booth alone vs a beat-up Camry to Denny's with five best friends; we live like the first. No partner is perfect; decide which "stats" you'll trade. "Figuring out what you want is 99% of the work." [▶ 1:45:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=6300s)
- **Decision-making is the highest-leverage skill** · Start with "what do I want to have happen?" (Bartlett's teenage list: Range Rover, a million, a six-pack, before 25.) We only want what we don't have, because punishment fades and reward sticks. [▶ 1:48:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=6480s)
- **Becoming a father** · Leila is pregnant (son due in about four months as of recording). He's wrestling with how to define a good parent and a successful child. Bartlett suggests focusing on inputs (water and sunlight for a plant); Alex still wants to know what he's optimising toward but settles on giving his kids as many skills as possible to get what they want from life. What he loves most about Leila: she never tried to change him. [▶ 1:50:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=6640s)
- **Funeral tweet (Feb 2025)** · He thinks about death multiple times a day and finds it positively correlated with his wellbeing. Wellbeing is a U-curve: kids and the elderly don't care what others think. He's trying to see the world as he will at 80 and pull that forward. [▶ 1:57:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=7040s)
- **Hardest quarter in eight years** · Q1 2025: business fine, but nine open lawsuits and Leila's serious injury with an ~18-month recovery. Ackman (via Alex): you can't solve it in a day; take one bite at a time and look back every month or two. Focus on the two feet in front of you. [▶ 2:00:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=7200s)
- **The four vectors of mental toughness** · Written for himself after his mother died suddenly (an accident), about four weeks after his ~$106M $100M Money Models launch that she got to see: 1) fortitude: how much bad can happen before your behaviour changes; 2) tolerance: how low you go when you fall; 3) resilience: how fast you return to baseline; 4) adaptability: afterwards, are you better, the same or worse? He rejects "you must suffer to prove your love"; she wouldn't want that. He changed as little as possible: kept making content, helping businesses and training because they made him feel better. "Why does the way I mourn have to look like yours?" Continuing the path she saw him start is how he honours her. [▶ 2:03:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=7381s)
- **On happiness** · He doesn't really know what it means; he's intensely interested in his life and it feels good to be him more days than not. Arthur Brooks on strivers: often an immigrant-parent childhood where approval is earned, so you get addicted to the earning loop. About half of wellbeing is genetic (Brooks); you can't see someone's "happiness height". He aggressively wants to keep living. Camus: the meaning of your life is the reason you don't end it (kids, spouse, people relying on you). He won't sell happiness; he sells quantifiable things. He's proud of the books; he writes them to outlive him. [▶ 2:09:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=7770s)
- **Bottom-10% days are statistics** · Feelings are weather. In a year, ~36 days will be bottom-10% days for no reason, three a month; also about one top-10% day a week. "My emotional discomfort is not an adequate reason to change what I'm doing." If you don't like your life in general, change something; if you don't like today, don't break up with your wife, give it a day. Founders wreck fledgling businesses acting on a bad day. A bad day where you still do good work is a good day. [▶ 2:16:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=8190s)
- **If superintelligence is a few years away** · Business: build as much real-world proof and track record with as many customers as possible: trust and distribution won't stop mattering. Personal: think hard about what it means to be human. [▶ 2:19:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwmwyBgzj8c&t=8340s)

lessons.t: 2026 · Ed Mylett Show · The Most Valuable 64 Minutes (Hormozi x Mylett, 2026) · 20 ideas
lessons.md:
> Watch it: [Ed Mylett Show · The Most Valuable 64 Minutes (Hormozi x Mylett, 2026)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6EmhvQgBh4). 20 ideas, paraphrased in my words; ▶ jumps to the minute.

- **Fatherhood shifts** · With his son Edward on the way: he's getting ahead on his son's education (doesn't like the system), and for the first time thinks about leaving wealth to someone rather than writing one cheque to charity; until now money was "chips to play the game". He and Leila nearly had kids at 28/25; they're all-or-nothing, so now hope for many. [▶ 2:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6EmhvQgBh4&t=125s)
- **Compress wake-to-work** · Your freshest processing is soon after waking (population-wide; know your own n=1). He minimises the gap: caffeine, nicotine, protein, creatine, then straight into work. In go-go seasons he trains at day's end (brain tired, body fresh). His sword to fall on: a routine must be a preference, never a crutch; he must be able to win without it. Invictus: "No one is ever 100%." Champions win despite imperfect conditions. [▶ 6:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6EmhvQgBh4&t=363s)
- **Unconditional effort** · (Mylett: most people's effort depends on conditions.) Alex: 1) once you start winning, beating others is too low a bar, so play against yourself (Andy Frisella's "100 to 0", leave no doubt); 2) after selling Gym Launch, a miserable year off gave him "work is the goal": judge yourself by how hard you worked relative to how hard you could work. Only you know that, which is gratifying and terrifying: you can win in the world's eyes and lose in your own. [▶ 10:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6EmhvQgBh4&t=630s)
- **Run up the score** · The $100M Money Models launch beat Prince Harry's 24-hour record (~1.4M copies, ~$43M) in about three hours; he kept going with almost no celebration: "we're not going to waste this attention", aiming for $100M. Both he and Mylett celebrate max-effort days, not result days. [▶ 13:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6EmhvQgBh4&t=785s)
- **Top 10 days → good-day formula** · Looking back at his top 10 days of the year: on his wall: "Focus is subtraction" and his good-day formula: work out with people you like, eat with people you like, write something. The result: nothing left in the tank, "I've earned my shower"; a day as a microcosm of a life left all on the field. People mistake the capacity this builds for talent. [▶ 16:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6EmhvQgBh4&t=962s)
- **Rest and an empty calendar** · Not anti-rest: five of seven days have almost nothing on them (half a day of meetings, one filming day). Two weeks ago he couldn't know what matters most today; open time let him assemble a ~$400M stock deal over six hours of calls on a Sunday. Maximise output over the longest horizon: in 24 hours take every stimulant; over a decade you must recover and stay aligned with meaning, family and purpose. Your 20s and 40s look different. [▶ 18:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6EmhvQgBh4&t=1110s)
- **Startup schedule** · Gym days, 12h × 6 days: innovation first (~4–10am, building assets that replicate a trainer, front desk, sales), then promotion and sales midday, admin last (billing, finance, broken equipment). Always a block working on the business, not in it. [▶ 22:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6EmhvQgBh4&t=1322s)
- **Control freak at the leverage point** · Jack Dorsey: "Perfect all the details, limit the number of details." Keep schedule flexibility to dive seven levels deep into the highest-leverage spot (show me the exact texts in this campaign), then zoom out. Elon attacks the "rate limiter" (constraint). Entrepreneurs are allocators of tiny resources; focus is subtraction: prune or everything becomes weeds. Most of his "control" is getting the team to do less. [▶ 24:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6EmhvQgBh4&t=1470s)
- **Three anti-human traits** · We like new, now and easy; entrepreneurship needs the opposite: focus (the old thing for a long time), patience (long horizon) and frustration tolerance (try again 100 times). He'd bet on a not-so-smart founder who can't abandon a task, has an unlimited horizon and never sells. "Your business isn't scaling for lack of information but for lack of character." [▶ 27:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6EmhvQgBh4&t=1620s)
- **Human patterns beat trend patterns** · If he had to pick, he'd train entrepreneurs to read human behaviour: humans unlock everything, even with AI. [▶ 29:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6EmhvQgBh4&t=1747s)
- **AI isn't the only leverage** · Many very wealthy people aren't vibe-coding 12 hours a day. Killing a wrong initiative gives back more time than AI-maxing it. Founders use AI to do dumb things fast, take on more, lose focus, and spend more on tokens without making more money. Picking one great person is huge leverage; AI is a tool in the toy box; it still can't make the call (you can prompt it to yes or no). [▶ 30:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6EmhvQgBh4&t=1801s)
- **Leadership = define and model the standard** · Leila is the internal leader, he's the external one; his only direct report is his father-in-law. Leadership steps: 1) define what good looks like in observable terms, 2) model it (Gandhi waited 30 days to quit sugar before telling a child to). Staff feedback: you can't witness consistency until you see him at the office at 6am six days a week. He's preparing for Leila stepping away completely for motherhood; he'll need to relearn the yin-yang balance. [▶ 33:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6EmhvQgBh4&t=1980s)
- **Raise the bet as you grow** · Getty, Rockefeller, Musk repeatedly pushed all chips back in at local maximums, both for bigger payoffs and to keep the game interesting: a billionaire playing $10 hands loses money. Risk tolerance must rise with the opportunity; capital becomes a moat because others won't risk it. [▶ 37:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6EmhvQgBh4&t=2223s)
- **The $1–3M swamp** · At Acquisition.com, $1–5M is "the swamp": it takes more risk to get out than to get in. Personal needs are met, and the next step means betting half your profit on one hire. Example: $2M at 20% margin → ~$300k usable; a real director costs $150–250k. You must go from $1k to $10k a day on ads, or pay a $35k headhunter. (Mylett: people look for any way out of the room rather than take that risk.) [▶ 41:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6EmhvQgBh4&t=2466s)
- **Lever up demand, conversion, delivery** · To de-risk the jump: demand (a content wheel where customers make content that brings customers), conversion (sell one-to-many and preload buyers with info so reps make "six-inch putts", trainable in a week), delivery (email/chat vs phone, async vs scheduled calls, recorded vs live, remote vs in person, one-to-group vs one-to-one: same buy rate, 3× capacity). None of these require AI; common sense first. [▶ 44:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6EmhvQgBh4&t=2641s)
- **Fear exists in the vague** · Write the plan B (his: Uber 12h a day plus stripping, ~$250k in a year, then restart). You only lose status with people not taking your risk, whose lives you don't want. Failure and success are on the same road; failure is just an earlier exit, so it's closer to success than thinking about success. Sales: "Let's get some noes today." [▶ 50:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6EmhvQgBh4&t=3004s)
- **Pattern recognition: assemble, don't build** · Replaying a video game takes a tenth of the time because you know the patterns. Your second business grows faster. Every role (first salesperson, sales manager) means failing until one works; then that becomes your pattern. Eventually "you don't build businesses, you assemble them," plus a network built by doing right by people. [▶ 52:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6EmhvQgBh4&t=3120s)
- **Anticipation is leverage** · First movers get more for less. A Gary Vee clip (regret not spending more on early AdWords) made Alex ask "what would it take to spend more?" on early Facebook ads. Bet on what won't change (Bezos); humans will still eat and need shelter. [▶ 57:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6EmhvQgBh4&t=3423s)
- **Personal risk dials** · Push vs pivot and how much to take off the table are personal. He takes chips off into boring things (real estate) so his family's oxygen mask is on; living very cheap young built a nest egg that let him take huge swings (Skool, the launch) where the worst case is his life doesn't change. [▶ 1:00:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6EmhvQgBh4&t=3600s)
- **What will this change about my day?** · His most practical risk filter: will this make me start doing things I don't want, or stop things I do? Most decisions don't change his day, so the stakes are imaginary; an upset wife changes his day more than almost any business setback, which reorders priorities. [▶ 1:01:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D6EmhvQgBh4&t=3690s)

lessons.t: 2026 · Ed Mylett Show · The Ultimate Guide to Building an Insanely Profitable Business (1h40, recorded 2022, reposted Dec 2023) · 24 ideas
lessons.md:
> Watch it: [Ed Mylett Show · The Ultimate Guide to Building an Insanely Profitable Business (1h40, recorded 2022, reposted Dec 2023)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M). 24 ideas, paraphrased in my words; ▶ jumps to the minute.

- **Opportunity = units × margin × competition** · Output = volume × time × leverage; work comes first, then opportunity is the next lever. Judge an opportunity by how many units you could sell, the gross-margin potential and the competitive dynamics. Telecom has huge demand and ~100% marginal margin but is capital-locked; a young, fast-growing market (cannabis then) gives you tailwinds. Buffett: what boat you're in matters more than how hard you row. Choosing the opportunity is the biggest leverage point in a career. [▶ 0:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=0s)
- **Should you change boats?** · Five years from retirement, keep compounding. With one or two entrepreneurial cycles left, weigh opportunity cost: give up two years of earnings to make 5× three years from now? The younger you are, the more you should take those bets. In inflation, favour low-capex, high-cash-flow businesses so price rises drop to the bottom line (Buffett). [▶ 3:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=185s)
- **Leverage defined** · The gap between inputs and outputs: a froyo job = low leverage; a few calls that make $10M on a deal = high leverage. Anything that increases output per unit of effort (a dialer, putting a podcast on YouTube, transcribing media). Naval's four types: labour (buy others' time: pay $10/h so you can sell at $50/h; early on you work double: your job plus earning their wage), capital, code, media. Buying time back is useless unless you spend it on higher-leverage work. [▶ 5:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=300s)
- **Use the cards you're dealt** · If your cards are anger, fear and disappointment, use them. "Let life beat the strength out of you or into you." Stop the contest over who had the sadder upbringing. His dad (a doctor, "why not a brain surgeon?"): he escalated goals (match dad's income → beat it → beat his lifetime earnings) until it was beyond reproach, then simply asked how big it can get. (Mylett: change the lever as you grow, like Jordan playing for the kid who'll see him once.) [▶ 11:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=662s)
- **The grandfather frame** · He'd trade all his future billions to be 32 again, even picking up trash; his 42-year-old self would trade everything for today. Imagine waking at 85 back in this body with your young wife, and today's business problems look "cute". Also the frame of the veteran (if it happened 1,000 times, you'd shrug). Their cat died at two; reframed: "what if cats lived six months? I got four times longer," turning sorrow into gratitude and cutting emotional reactivity. Keeps the main thing the main thing: at 85 he'll care about people helped, not money made. [▶ 17:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=1020s)
- **Simple scales, fancy fails** · The everyday urgency blueprint = "do the boring work": repeat successful actions. If it worked once, it'll work again; people change what works. Scale adds complexity on its own (100 → 10,000 calls); don't add more. Only two ways to make more: sell more units or make them worth more. [▶ 23:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=1380s)
- **Hold contradictions** · You already believe in justice and mercy, variety and consistency. Wisdom is knowing which to use when. (Mylett: fear isn't negative; too much of it is.) [▶ 26:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=1560s)
- **Broke again: control the controllables** · After losing the gym money: he could market and sell, so he did. Launching Gym Launch with six recruited reps, he put ~$3,300/day on an Amex with a $100k limit and $1,000 in the bank, with no payment processor while contracts piled up; a $50k/month processor arrived in the last week; he ran $50k on 28 Jan and $50k on 1 Feb to cover the month. His refrain: "I cannot lose if I do not quit." You judge a life only at the end. [▶ 28:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=1680s)
- **Scarcity = cut supply** · Supply and demand are the two forces; marketing pushes demand, but cutting supply is underused. A luxury jeweller at a charity event: "Whenever demand increases, cut supply." If you 100× volume tomorrow you couldn't handle it anyway, so state the real cap ("I only take 10 clients"): it pulls customers in and stops you overextending. Sales: there's always a cost of inaction accumulating; direct attention to it. Use it ethically and truthfully or you'll wreck your reputation. [▶ 34:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=2047s)
- **Scarcity vs urgency** · Scarcity = limited units; urgency = limited time ("this promotion ends tomorrow"). Even with unlimited protein: a limited flavour, or a bonus (workout template) only this month, adding value and scarcity at once. [▶ 39:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=2346s)
- **Trim and stack** · List every problem prospects have (micro-steps included) → turn each into a solution → choose delivery vehicles with the delivery cube (ratio 1:1/group/many; speed of response; quality: frontline vs VIP; medium: zoom/in person/phone/chat) → write the cost of each → keep the high-value, low-cost ones, trim the rest → bundle, then add scarcity, bonuses, guarantee, urgency. [▶ 41:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=2463s)
- **Product is the multiplier** · Naval: "You only sell because you don't know how to market, and you only market because you don't know how to build a product." Five ways to get customers: cold outreach, content, paid ads, affiliates/partners (all linear) and referrals (compounding). CAC and operational drag rise over time; only referrals counteract them. $100M Offers sold 200k+ copies in year one from one post, no ads. Rhythm: one product, one avatar, one channel to $1–3M; then pause acquisition and fix the product until referrals flow, and you'll "sneeze your way to $10M"; then scale acquisition again. [▶ 45:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=2702s)
- **After fixing the product, crush every channel** · With higher LTV from word of mouth, you can outspend everyone who bulldozed to $10M on low LTV: then build cold email, cold call, paid ad, affiliate and partner teams. [▶ 50:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=3030s)
- **What a lead is** · A lead = a person you can contact; what people really want is engaged leads (contactable and showing interest in what you sell). Unengaged → engaged → qualified → customer. $100M Leads covers only the jump from stranger to raised hand. [▶ 52:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=3126s)
- **Core Four + Lead Getters** · One-to-one vs one-to-many × people who know you vs don't: warm outreach, cold outreach, content, paid ads. These are the only ways to make something known. Lead getters do them on your behalf: customers (referrals; needs an exceptional product), affiliates, agencies, employees. One hire (a director of people) created a team that posted ~300 pieces a week and picked the ad agency. The launch: ~137k from paid ads, ~104k from affiliates (27k signed up), ~200k from content, the rest referrals; 500k registered, ~200k live. Like a "How to market a book" book with 14 reviews proves its author can't. [▶ 54:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=3240s)
- **Channels assist each other** · Cold call → they check your profile and content before the close; without content you'd blame "bad cold calling" for a lost sale. Pick one channel to start; all four work better together. Works for any sales cycle (realtor example: warm, cold, listings content, ads, home-service partner referrals, past clients, agencies, team). [▶ 1:01:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=3660s)
- **Need money tomorrow? Warm outreach** · Export every contact (email, phone, social) into one sheet. Open each with something personal about their life (new baby, Tough Mudder), not your offer; use ACA: acknowledge, compliment (and label them with a trait you'll use later), ask the next question; steer to your topic; book a 10-minute qualification call. [▶ 1:06:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=3967s)
- **CLOSER framework** · Clarify why they're here ("just want info" — no, what problem? what do you want in 6 months?); Label them with the problem (200 lb → wants 130: that's the gap); Overview past experiences (the pain cycle: what did you try, like, dislike? past pain raises importance; note what they liked for your pitch); Sell the vacation, not the plane flight (Maui, not TSA and seat numbers); Explain away concerns (the onion: circumstances like time/money/fit → other people/decision-makers → themselves); Reinforce the decision. For bigger tickets, stop the set call mid-pain with an "integrity tie-down" and do CLOSER again on call two. Their 17-item lead-nurture checklist lifts show rates to ~85% even on cold prospects (each item +5–7%). [▶ 1:09:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=4141s)
- **Reinforce: choreograph 24 hours** · Back-outs happen: the moment the card clears, text from onboarding or a warm handoff. Set expectations, meet them; just keep your word. Hack: during a 14-day onboarding, send a daily "no reply needed: we did these three things" so by day 7 it's the eighth touch, not the first: lower back-outs, more ascensions and referrals. (Mylett nearly lost a nine-figure deal by missing that window.) [▶ 1:15:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=4506s)
- **Train the script back to front** · A rep who knows only the close can still close; one who knows only rapport can't. Everything is questions until you sell the vacation; obstacles (before the ask: "just info", other decision makers — handled in nurture) vs objections (after: time, money, fit, decision maker, fear). Loop back to the close after each; when they say yes, stop selling: "Great, which card?" [▶ 1:20:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=4805s)
- **Framing = contextualising** · Pre-frame, frame, post-frame. Translate jargon into what it means ("your house is protected; you sleep at night"). The launch built a ~$112k value stack, price-dropped and then gave it away: ~200 hours on the presentation vs ~2,000 on the book. [▶ 1:22:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=4922s)
- **No one's coming to save you** · Power follows the blame finger (at 19 he was giving his mother his leash). "The first two words out of poverty are 'my fault'": it may not be your fault but it's your problem. Operationalise through actions not feelings: make 100 calls whether you love it or hate it. You can get it without deserving it; "the iron is the iron". Someone will save you: future you. [▶ 1:27:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=5226s)
- **Rocky with no music** · The cut-scene is two minutes in the film and five years in life, with no soundtrack and no certainty. A guarantee would make it worthless. (Mylett: his nephew's detailing business: knock 100 doors every Saturday; doing the ugly shrinks fear because the maths says you'll win.) [▶ 1:31:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=5463s)
- **Input-output equation and emotions** · Boil any goal down to a number of actions (dials, emails, DMs, posts, ad spend) and plug and chug: action alleviates anxiety. Sadness = perceived lack of options (solve with knowledge); anxiety = many options, no priorities (solve with a decision). His highest-ROI habit: the first six hours of every day on moving the business forward; no meetings, no calls. His team books meetings from 4pm backwards. Not getting enough leads? "You're not advertising enough. Period." [▶ 1:34:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvEhPIRtk9M&t=5641s)

lessons.t: 2026 · 1/0 Live #2 · Advice for Achieving Your Goals Faster Than Everyone (Feb 2024, 1h30) · 18 ideas
lessons.md:
> Watch it: [1/0 Live #2 · Advice for Achieving Your Goals Faster Than Everyone (Feb 2024, 1h30)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9OsUfwTTslc). 18 ideas, paraphrased in my words; ▶ jumps to the minute.

- **Goals on controllables** · Short or long outcome goals are both uncontrollable; set goals on activities you can control and measure the percentage of days you did them. A new gym-goer's program is binary: did you go? Month one, count the days; then add things. Hit 100% of your activities and miss the outcome and you still kept your word, which builds confidence. [▶ 2:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9OsUfwTTslc&t=123s)
- **The ACQ goal sheet** · Column 1: what problem are we solving, and does it chunk up to more customers, more value per customer, or less risk of either (enterprise value)? Column 2: hypothesis "if we do X, Y will happen". Columns 3–4: X (input) and Y (output). After the period: did we do X? Did Y happen? If we did X and Y didn't, amend the hypothesis (e.g. double videos but keep quality). If the team did everything they committed to and outcomes missed, that's fine. [▶ 4:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9OsUfwTTslc&t=243s)
